The Office objected to claim 19 for including two instances of "wherein". The claim language has been amended to delete one instance of the word. Therefore, Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner withdraw the objection. IV. Rejection Under 35 U.S.C. § 102
The Office rejected claims 1-10 and 12-25 under 35 U.S.C. § 102 as allegedly anticipated by Anderson et al. Office Action, 2. Applicant respectfully traverses the rejection.

"A claim is anticipated only if each and every element as set forth in the claim is found, either expressly or inherently described, in a single prior art reference." MPEP § 2131 (quoting Verdegaal Bros. v. Union Oil Co. of California, 814 F.2d 628, 631 (Fed. Cir. 1987)) (internal quotations omitted). Furthermore, "[t]he identical invention must be shown in as complete detail as is contained in the . . . claim." See id. (quoting Richardson v. Suzuki Motor Co., 868 F.2d 1226, 1236 (Fed. Cir. 1989)). However, Anderson et al. fails to teach Applicant's claim 1 and 23-25. Nevertheless, solely to advance prosecution and without acquiescing to the rejection, Applicant amends claims
1 and 23-25 to further distinguish them from Anderson et al.
Applicant submits that Anderson et al. does not teach each element of the

subject matter recited by the unamended pending claims. For example, claim 1 recites "receiving first sensor data indicating at least one attribute of high voltage wiring of the aircraft." The Office asserts that Anderson et al. teaches this subject matter, citing Anderson et al. at paragraph [0271], which describes that "[a] triplexer also routes data from the vehicle to the control station including sensor data, payload data and telemetry from the aerial vehicle to the control station." Office Action pgs. 3-4. Anderson et al., however, does not disclose that its "sensor data, payload data and telemetry" "indicat[es] at least one attribute of high voltage wiring of the aircraft," as recited by claim 1 (emphasis added). Claim 1 is therefore distinct from Anderson et al. for this first reason.
Additionally, claim 1 recites "determine ... a proximity of a temperature of the

high voltage wiring to a temperature limit based on the first sensor data and the state of operation of the aircraft." The Office asserts that Anderson et al. teaches this subject matter, citing Anderson et al. at paragraphs [0175], [0177], and [0178]. Office Action pg.

4. However, these paragraphs of Anderson et al. are directed to testing a cooling system for a HiPer spooler. Paragraphs [0173]-[0178] detail procedures for "experimental tests" and paragraph [0178] ultimately concludes that "the cooling appeared to be adequate in the flat spool design." There is no determination of "a proximity of a temperature of the high voltage wiring to a temperature limit," let alone a determination of this proximity being "based on the first sensor data and the state of operation of the aircraft." Additionally, even if the testing procedures in Anderson et al. disclosed determining a proximity, which Applicant does not concede, there is no

indication that the proximity is used, as recited in the claims, for "controlling at least one electric propulsion unit of the aircraft to avoid exceeding the temperature limit based on the determined proximity" (emphasis added).
Solely to advance prosecution and without agreeing or acquiescing to any

position taken in the Office Action, Applicant has amended the claim language to state that the receiving and determining steps are performed "during flight", as discussed in the Examiner interview. In Anderson et al. there is no indication that the proximity is determined "during flight" or based on first sensor data and a state of operation of the aircraft received "during flight". In fact, Anderson et al. describes "experimental tests" (Anderson et al. at [0175]) in a lab setting, as depicted in Fig. 13E and throughout the reference.

In view of the above, Anderson et al. fails to teach the subject matter of amended claim 1. Accordingly, claim 1 is allowable over Anderson et al. Independent claims 23-25, although different in scope from claim 1, recite similar subject matter, so they are also allowable for at least the same reasons. Claims 2-22 each depend from claim 1 and are allowable over the cited references by at least virtue of their respective dependencies. These claims also recite additional elements distinguishing them over the art of record.
For at least these reasons, Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner
withdraw the rejections of claims 1-10 and 12-25 under 35 U.S.C. § 102 and allow the claims.
V. Rejections Under 35 U.S.C. § 103

Applicant respectfully traverses the rejections of claim 11 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly unpatentable over the asserted combination of Anderson et al. and Hirono. Office Action at pgs. 19-21. No prima facie case of obviousness has been established for at least the reason that the Office Action has neither properly determined the scope and content of the prior art nor properly ascertained the differences between the prior art and the claimed combinations.

The Office cited Anderson et al. in the rejection of claim 11. This claim depends from claim 1 which, as noted above, has been amended with subject matter that Anderson et al. fails to disclose. Hirono fails to cure the above-noted deficiencies of Anderson et al. Accordingly, claim 11 is allowable over the cited references by at least virtue of its dependence.
For at least these reasons, Applicant respectfully requests that the Examiner withdraw the rejection of claims 11 under 35 U.S.C. § 103 and allow the claim. VI. Conclusion

In view of the foregoing, Applicant respectfully requests reconsideration of this application, withdrawal of the claim rejections, and the timely allowance of the pending claims.
